Right: lattice_reference(seed=1) keeps every degree but only accepts swaps that shorten edges around the ring A to H: the four long accent edges on the left become the four short accent edges on the right, closing four triangles around the ring, and the average clustering rises to 0.667." width="100%"} Like `random_reference()`, this rewires the graph with degree-preserving double edge swaps, but only accepts swaps that make the edges shorter on a ring of the nodes (nodes placed on a circle in ID order). The result approaches a ring lattice with the original degree sequence: highly clustered, with long paths. It is the "ordered" baseline of `small_world_omega()`. The graph is treated as undirected and simple. With `connectivity=True`, swaps that would disconnect the graph are undone. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [niter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[5]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Rewiring rounds, each attempting one swap per edge (default 5). [connectivity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), keep the graph connected. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducible results. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected, unweighted graph with the same nodes and rewired edges. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or has fewer than four nodes or two edges. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Sporns and Zwi (2004) latticize by accepting a swap of `a-b, c-d` into `a-d, c-b` only when the ring distances satisfy $d(a, d) + d(c, b) \le d(a, b) + d(c, d)$. NetworkX's `lattice_reference` instead compares $d(a, c) + d(b, d)$, which does not measure the new edges; EdgeCase uses the intended criterion, so its references are more lattice-like. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Latticizing a random graph raises its clustering: ::: {#f2e9f69b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_gnp_graph(n=40, p=0.15, seed=3) lattice = g.lattice_reference(niter=10, seed=4) ( round(g.get_avg_clustering_coefficient(), 3), round(lattice.get_avg_clustering_coefficient(), 3), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.147, 0.6) ``` ::: :::
